conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the medicine team. I want to check in after your fall and passing out. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired. My stomach is burning like always, and my left knee hurts from the fall. I’m scared it’s a seizure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense to worry about. From what you and your son described—standing up, room spinning, then passing out—this could be from low blood volume and low blood pressure when you stand, especially with how little you’ve been able to drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I barely get down water. Since the hiatal hernia surgery, I can’t tolerate anything. Even protein shakes make me nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that in the ER—your heart rate was low at first, and you were dehydrated. We’re going to keep giving IV fluids and check orthostatic vitals—blood pressure and pulse lying, sitting, and standing—to see if they drop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the slurred speech I had this morning? That freaked me out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We took that seriously. The CT and the CT angiogram of your head and neck didn’t show a stroke, bleeding, or a blocked artery. Neurology also examined you and thinks a neurologic emergency is unlikely, but they’ll stay involved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a stroke?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on the imaging, there’s no evidence of an acute stroke. We’ll still monitor you closely, especially because you’ve had dizziness and a seizure history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My stomach pain is worse since that surgery. It’s like burning right here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Your CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis didn’t show an obstruction or anything acute, which is reassuring. Given your history of marginal ulcers and chronic nausea/vomiting, we’re going to focus on acid suppression and nausea control while we figure out nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to NSAIDs and aspirin. Please don’t give me those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for saying that—we have it listed, and we won’t give NSAIDs. We’ll use acetaminophen and other options for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My knee—did I break it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The knee X-ray didn’t show a fracture, and there wasn’t an effusion seen. We’ll treat it with acetaminophen and a lidocaine patch and keep an eye on swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing: your head/neck scan incidentally noted a very small lung nodule—4 millimeters. It’s not causing your symptoms, but we’ll recommend follow-up imaging in about 12 months if you’re considered high risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A lung nodule? Does that mean cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most nodules that small are benign. The recommendation is just to consider a repeat CT in a year depending on risk factors. We’ll put it in your discharge plan so it doesn’t get lost.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Overnight, did you have any more dizziness when you stood up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. When I got up to the bathroom, I felt like I was going to black out again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your orthostatic vitals are still positive—your blood pressure drops when you stand. That supports dehydration and low circulating volume as the main cause. We’ll continue IV fluids and encourage small sips as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But sipping hurts. It makes the burning worse and then I throw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We tried antacids and an H2 blocker, but given your symptoms we’re switching to pantoprazole twice a day, which is stronger acid suppression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that different from my omeprazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same class of medication, but we’re using pantoprazole at a higher, scheduled dose twice daily to calm irritation and help ulcers heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I going to need another feeding tube? Last time it went wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not rushing into anything. First we want GI to evaluate why swallowing and intake are so hard right now. Nutrition will also see you today to assess malnutrition risk and options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Neurology reviewed your case again. They still think this episode is more consistent with syncope than a seizure, but given your history they recommend EEG monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does the EEG involve? Is it painful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not painful. Sticky electrodes go on your scalp to record brain waves. We’re looking for seizure activity while you’re awake and asleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EEG so far looks normal—no seizures captured and no epileptiform activity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why do I get that spinning feeling like before a seizure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That spinning can come from low blood pressure, inner ear issues, or less commonly neurologic causes. Because your exam raised some concern, neurology recommended an MRI of the brain to be thorough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We have the MRI result: it’s normal—no stroke or mass. There’s a tiny benign-appearing cyst remnant in the right hippocampal area that isn’t an acute finding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… that’s a relief. But I still feel weak when I stand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. The main driver still seems to be low intake and dehydration. We’ll keep working on fluids and nutrition, and we’ll have physical therapy help with safe ambulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How is the nausea today? Any vomiting overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I threw up once. The burning pain is constant. I’m afraid to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to restart metoclopramide to help stomach emptying, since gastroparesis has been part of your history. We held it initially because of a prolonged QT concern, but we think the benefit outweighs the risk now and we’ll monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve tried so many meds. What if nothing works?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If medications aren’t enough, the next step is to look directly with an endoscopy to see if there’s narrowing or irritation that we can treat. GI is planning that evaluation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update: despite fluids, you’re still getting lightheaded at times. This can happen when the body’s autonomic system doesn’t adjust well. If it persists after nutrition improves, neurology recommends outpatient autonomic testing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that like a tilt table test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly—tests that measure how your heart rate and blood pressure respond to position changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI is planning the endoscopy for tomorrow to evaluate the burning pain and poor intake. The goal is to see if there’s inflammation or a narrowing that can be treated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous. Will I be awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get sedation so you’re comfortable and usually don’t remember it. GI will review the risks and benefits with you beforehand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The endoscopy is done. GI found a narrowing at the anastomotic junction and some irritation in the stomach. They dilated the narrowing with a balloon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I can’t get anything down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It likely contributed. The dilation should help, but it can take time, and irritation can still cause pain and nausea. We’re continuing pantoprazole twice daily, and we’re adding sucralfate to coat and protect the lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I have an ulcer again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They saw irritation and we’re treating it like ulcer-type injury with strong acid suppression and sucralfate. The key is protecting the area and avoiding things that worsen it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had watery diarrhea since last night. I’m worried about C. diff again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, that’s a reasonable concern. We sent a stool test for C. difficile.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your C. difficile PCR came back negative, which is good. We’ll keep monitoring your stools and hydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you doing with clear liquids today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A few sips, but I still get nauseous. I’m not meeting anything close to what I need.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what nutrition is seeing too—your intake is far below what your body needs, and that’s contributing to weakness and dizziness. We need a reliable way to get nutrition in while your stomach heals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you talking about a tube again? I’m terrified it’ll be misplaced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. The plan being discussed is a post-pyloric feeding tube—a dobhoff—placed with endoscopic guidance so it goes beyond the stomach. It’s different from the prior situation, and we’ll confirm placement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Would I still be able to drink anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—GI and nutrition will guide it, but generally we keep you on liquids by mouth as tolerated and use the tube to meet protein and calorie needs. We’ll also avoid solid foods for now while things heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your dizziness is improving some—your blood pressures are more stable, though you still get a bit tachycardic when walking. That fits with recovery from low volume, but we’ll keep watching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My anxiety is through the roof. I feel like my body is failing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This is a lot to go through. We’ll continue your home medications for anxiety and depression, and you can use lorazepam as needed for anxiety and nausea. We’ll also keep you updated step by step so nothing feels like it’s happening to you without you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI and the bariatric surgery team reviewed your case with us. Given ongoing poor intake despite dilation and medications, we think the safest next step is to place the post-pyloric dobhoff and start tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long would I have it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s meant as a bridge to get you nutritionally stable. Long-term planning—like whether you need a more permanent feeding access—should be decided with your bariatric surgeon who did the hiatal hernia repair, since they know your anatomy best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today is the tube placement. It will be done endoscopically, and afterward we’ll start tube feeds slowly and increase as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt my throat? And what if I gag?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You may have some throat and nose discomfort at first, but we’ll use numbing and sedation during placement. If you feel nauseated afterward, we’ll treat that and adjust the feeding rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The post-pyloric dobhoff is in place, and we started tube feeds. We’re going to advance the rate gradually while monitoring for nausea, abdominal pain, and electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can feel it in my nose. It’s uncomfortable, but I’m glad something is finally happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did you tolerate the feeds overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better than I expected. Some nausea, but not like when I try to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. We’ll keep pantoprazole twice daily and sucralfate, and continue metoclopramide with meals if you take anything by mouth. For pain, we’ll prioritize acetaminophen and avoid anything that worsens nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting discharge planning. The plan is for you to go home with services and continue tube feeds. Before you leave, we’ll secure the tube with a bridle so it’s less likely to come out accidentally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Who teaches me how to use it? I don’t want to mess it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our nursing team and the home infusion/tube feed service will teach you how to run the feeds, flush the tube, and troubleshoot alarms. We’ll also give you clear instructions on when to call for help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, avoid solid foods while your gut heals. Stick to liquids as tolerated—high-protein options like nutrition shakes—while the tube feeds provide the bulk of your nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the dizziness and the spinning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s improved as your hydration improved, but because you’ve had vertigo sensations before, neurology recommends outpatient autonomic testing and an ENT evaluation. They also want you to follow up with neurology for possible further seizure characterization.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge day check-in: your vitals are stable, you’re walking independently, and you’ve been tolerating tube feeds. Your abdominal exam is similar—some epigastric tenderness but no concerning signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still worried I’ll pass out again at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. The biggest prevention is hydration and nutrition. Stand up slowly, sit at the edge of the bed before walking, and if you feel dizzy, sit or lie down right away. If you faint again, have chest pain, shortness of breath, or new neurologic symptoms, come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What medications am I leaving with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your home meds including levetiracetam for seizures, fluoxetine and aripiprazole, zolpidem at night, and ondansetron as needed. New or emphasized meds include pantoprazole twice daily and sucralfate twice daily for stomach irritation. You’ll also have folic acid daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with GI for management of the feeding tube, and with your primary care doctor to help monitor tube feeds and nutrition. Follow up with your bariatric surgeon who did the hiatal hernia repair for the long-term feeding plan. Neurology follow-up for possible further seizure evaluation, plus outpatient autonomic testing and ENT for vertigo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If the tube clogs or I get worse pain, what do I do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call the home service and GI for tube issues, and come to the ER if you have fevers, chills, worsening abdominal pain, bleeding, persistent vomiting, worsening diarrhea, or if the tube dislodges and you can’t use it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, any last questions or concerns you want to make sure we address?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No—just… thank you for taking it seriously. I hope the feeds help me get my strength back.
